Hess and Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission (Compensation)

16 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2343Tribunal reviewEmployment & workplace
Martin Hess sought compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation (Defence-related Claims) Act 1988 (Cth) for lumbar spondylosis allegedly caused by his Australian Army Reserve service. The Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission denied liability, and Mr Hess sought review by the Tribunal. The Tribunal affirmed the denial because it was not satisfied that military service contributed to a significant degree to the condition.
Key holding

For a disease to be compensable under the DRCA, the employee’s employment must have contributed to the ailment to a significant degree, meaning substantially more than material.

significant degree" means a degree that is substantially more than material.

Latif and Commissioner of the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission (Practice and procedure)

16 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2342Tribunal reviewVisa refusal review
The Tribunal refused the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission’s application to dismiss Mr Latif’s review applications concerning deemed internal review decisions to affirm a permanent ban and registration renewal refusal for Horizon Solsolutions Australia Pty Ltd. The case concerned whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction, whether Mr Latif was “directly affected”, and whether deemed decisions arose under the ART Act. The dismissal application was dismissed, so the substantive review applications remain on foot.
Key holding

A decision-maker cannot isolate a separate non-reviewable “standing” decision from the NDIS Act s 100 internal review process; standing is a threshold matter within that process and may be assessed by the Tribunal in determining jurisdiction.

It is my characterisation that the issue of standing is inherently a threshold matter that should be addressed as an integral part of the internal review process under s 100 of the NDIS Act, rather than as a distinct and, in this case as submitted by the Respondent, a non-reviewable decision made under s 100(2) of that Act.

Mishra and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

15 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2327Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Mishra’s Subclass 155 Five-Year Resident Return visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Mr Mishra accepted he did not pass the character test because of a 22-month aggregate sentence for family violence offences. The Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision after considering whether another reason existed under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) and Direction No. 110.
Key holding

Where a visa is mandatorily cancelled because the holder fails the character test due to a substantial criminal record, the Tribunal must consider whether there is another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), applying Direction No. 110.

In accordance with s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), the Tribunal must therefore consider whether there is another reason to exercise the discretion under s 501CA(4) to revoke the original decision.

Lye v Comcare

15 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1517Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationMigration
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.
Key holding

Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs

15 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1531Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationCharacter testMigration
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.
Key holding

A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

15 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1520Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.
Key holding

Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

CYZGC by his plan nominee and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure)

14 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2332Tribunal reviewVisa refusal review
The applicant, a 10-year-old NDIS participant, sought interim relief after a reassessment increased his core supports but reduced his therapy funding and added behaviour support. He asked the Tribunal under s 32(2) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth) to reallocate or make flexible the behaviour support funding, or alternatively to stay Plan-2 so Plan-1 revived. The Tribunal refused, finding neither order desirable to ensure the effectiveness of the review, and recommended an early conference and hearing.
Key holding

Under s 32(2) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), an interim stay or other order is made only if desirable to ensure the effectiveness of the review; hardship, even serious hardship, is insufficient unless it puts the effectiveness of the review in jeopardy.

Finally, in relation to hardship, it is not enough that the decision causes hardship, even serious hardship. The discretion may only be exercised where the degree of hardship is such that it puts the effectiveness of the review in jeopardy.[5]

Standard outdoor play equipment falling within item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules is not an NDIS support and cannot be funded unless it is modified or adapted to address the participant’s functional impairments.

LFQR and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security second review)

14 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2320Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewEmployment & workplace
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal to pay family tax benefit top ups and supplements for 2022/23 because the applicant’s partner lodged his income tax return on 4 July 2024, after the 30 June 2024 reconciliation deadline. The applicant relied on stress, family violence, alcohol issues, a brief separation and pandemic-related pressures. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no special circumstances that prevented the partner from lodging on time.
Key holding

Under s 32D(1)(c)(ii) of the Administration Act, special circumstances will only extend the reconciliation time if they actually prevented the partner from lodging the income tax return by the required date.

For the Applicant to be paid top ups and supplements of family tax benefit for 2022/23, the Tribunal must be satisfied that there are special circumstances that prevented the Applicant's partner from lodging his income tax return by 30 June 2024.

Jaworski v Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (No 2)

14 Oct 2026New South Wales Court of Appeal[2026] NSWCA 213Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Ward P; Harrison AJA Decision: 1. Dismiss the applicant’s application to set asi
Mr Jaworski sought to set aside or vary the Court of Appeal’s earlier leave judgment under UCPR r 36.16, and CA ANZ sought gross sum costs. The Court dismissed the reopening application and fixed costs at $30,000 for the leave/recusal application and $6,000 for CA ANZ’s notice of motion. The dispute concerned alleged errors, bias/prejudgment and costs in ongoing litigation involving CA ANZ.
Key holding

Under UCPR r 36.16, reopening requires some error in the court's reasoning due to misapprehension of fact or law that is not solely attributable to the applicant's neglect or default.

What is required to be established on an application under r 36.16 is some error in the court's reasoning because of a misapprehension of the facts or misapprehension of the relevant law; and that this misapprehension cannot be attributed solely to the neglect or default of the party seeking the rehearing.

The applicant sought review of several Taxation Office decisions concerning his income tax affairs, including invalid objection determinations. Key holding

A decision that is not a reviewable objection decision within s 14ZQ of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth) is not reviewable by the Tribunal under s 14ZZA, so the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction.

Coe and Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

13 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2317Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewCriminal law
Jason Coe applied to have Jardini Pty Ltd’s Great Barrier Reef Marine Park permit transferred to him personally. However it does believe that at this time, and having regard to the present circumstances, there are matters which are relevant to the proposed transfer and the objects of the GBRMP Act and management of the Marine Park such that the transfer of the Permit should not be approved.

Kay and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation and business)

13 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2310Tribunal reviewContracts
Matthew Kay objected to superannuation guarantee charge assessments for failing to make superannuation contributions for Daryl Marschke for 1 July 2019 to 30 June 2023. The Commissioner initially found Mr Marschke was not an employee but later reversed that position on delegation issues and assessed SGC. The Tribunal affirmed the objection decision.
Key holding

A contract is not wholly or principally for a person’s labour if it leaves the contractor free to do the work personally or employ others, even if the contractor in fact performs most of the work.

Even where a person has performed the bulk of the work under the contract, or it was the expectation of the parties that the person would do so, a contract that 'leaves the contractor free to do the work himself or employ other persons to carry it out' is not wholly or principally for the labour of the person.

South Australian Commission for Catholic Schools Inc and Secretary, Department of Education (Guidance and Appeals Panel)

13 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2304Tribunal reviewVisa nomination
The Tribunal reviewed 2024 Commonwealth recurrent funding determinations for 84 non-government Catholic schools in South Australia. It unanimously held that mid-year reception students who began in term 3 2024 were “primary students” because reception was the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1. A majority then held those students did not have a pattern of regular attendance at school or school generally during 2024, so they failed reg 9B(1)(c) and were ineligible unless the Minister included them under reg 9B(3).
Key holding

Reception undertaken by mid-year reception students is the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1, so those students are primary students in that calendar year.

Giving the phrases to which I have already referred their natural meaning, the logical conclusion is that the 2024 mid-year reception students were in the year of schooling in a course of primary education that was immediately before year 1. It follows that, in 2024, those students were in the foundation year of schooling, were receiving primary education and were therefore primary students at their school.

Tran and Australian Skills Quality Authority

12 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2300Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationAdministrative law
Mr Tran sought review of ASQA’s decision to cancel his Certificate III in Carpentry, obtained via RPL from Kingsway, a deregistered RTO. Although the Tribunal found the s 56(1)(a) ground was established because Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary assessment, it exercised the discretion not to cancel in exceptional circumstances. The cancellation decision was set aside and the qualification is to be treated as a valid VET RPL qualification.
Key holding

Even when the s 56(1)(a) ground is established, the Tribunal may exercise the s 56(1) discretion not to cancel a VET qualification in exceptional circumstances, including clear lack of applicant fault, misleading RTO conduct, extensive genuine industry experience, and a public interest that does not require cancellation.

The Tribunal is satisfied that the discretion under subsection 56(1) of the NVR Act not to cancel the Qualification can be safely and appropriately exercised in the exceptional circumstances of this case. That discretion may be exercised consistent with the public interest, given that Mr Tran possesses the requisite training, skills and work experience to have been awarded the Qualification on an RPL basis.

Comcare v Administrative Review Tribunal

8 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1481Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewEmployment & workplace
Comcare sought judicial review under s 39B of the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth) of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision refusing to release Comcare and Mr Sewell from the Harman obligation over summonsed medical records. Comcare wanted to use the records to manage Mr Sewell’s future SRC Act compensation claims after liability under s 14 was accepted by consent. The Federal Court dismissed the application, holding the Tribunal committed no jurisdictional error.
Key holding

The general functions, powers and decision-making provisions in the SRC Act do not impliedly exclude the Harman obligation for documents produced on summons in ART review proceedings concerning s 14 liability.

For these reasons, ss 69(a), 70 and 72 of the SRC Act (whether alone or in combination) do not establish a statutory inconsistency that would prevent the Harman obligation from applying to documents produced on a summons in Tribunal proceedings to determine liability under s 14 of the SRC Act.

It is not sufficient that the accessory merely knows that his or her conduct will assist the principal perpetrator in the commission of the offence.

The Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed a refusal of a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) Subclass 500 visa because Mr Dangilan did not satisfy the genuine temporary entrant criterion in cl 500.212(a). Key holding

To satisfy cl 500.212(a), the Tribunal must be affirmatively satisfied on the whole of the circumstances and Direction No 108 that the applicant genuinely intends a temporary stay; otherwise the criterion is not met.

On the basis of the above, the Tribunal is not satisfied that the applicant intends genuinely to stay in Australia temporarily. Accordingly, the applicant does not meet cl 500.212(a).

1 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2362Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
This case concerns a Subclass 485 (Temporary Graduate) visa applicant who mistakenly selected the Graduate Work stream but would have met the Post-Study Work stream criteria. The Tribunal held it was bound by Obinwa to assess only the stream selected on the visa application form. The delegate’s refusal was affirmed.
Key holding

An applicant who nominates a particular Subclass 485 stream must satisfy the criteria for that stream, and the Tribunal need not consider an alternative stream.

The consequence is that an applicant for a Class VC visa who nominates a particular stream (as every applicant must, in order to make a valid application) must satisfy the criteria applicable to that stream in order for the visa to be granted. Satisfying criteria that are applicable only to another stream does not assist.

This was a Full Court appeal about a disability support pension claim. Key holding

In assessing whether treatment is “reasonable treatment” under s 6(7) of the Impairment Tables Determination, “reasonable cost” requires consideration of whether the treatment is reasonably affordable to the claimant in their circumstances, not merely whether the cost is objectively reasonable in the market.

Before: P. Maishman

Key holding

2115044 (Refugee)

24 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3976Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Sue Zelinka
The applicant, a Macedonian citizen, sought review of a refusal of a protection visa based on feared harm from family and an alleged criminal gang after his secret marriage to his first cousin became known. The Tribunal accepted the marriage and societal stigma but found no real chance of serious harm, given the divorce, his father’s reconciliation, his second marriage, and that “Komiti” was a football supporters’ club. It affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

A particular social group claim cannot succeed where the asserted group is not cognisable because its defining marriage is unlawful in the receiving country, or where the group is defined only by a shared fear of persecution or family harm.

The Tribunal rejects this formulation noting that there is no such group because first cousins, by law, cannot marry in Macedonia and therefore there cannot be a large, cognisable group of them. Any other variation of particular social group involving victims of harm at family hands is also rejected because a particular social group cannot be constituted by persons bound only by fear of persecution.

Cai (Migration)

23 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3835Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Paul Windsor
Mr Cai applied for a Visitor (Class FA) subclass 600 visa in the Tourist stream. The delegate refused the visa because it was not satisfied he genuinely intended to stay temporarily in Australia under cl 600.211. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding his long continuous stay and unsupported medical claims indicated he was using the visitor visa to establish de facto residence.
Key holding

To satisfy cl 600.211, the applicant must positively satisfy the Tribunal of a genuine intention to stay temporarily for the visa purpose; a long continuous stay without a credible departure timeframe or supporting medical evidence can show the visitor visa is being used for de facto residence.

Given the applicant has been in Australia continuously since January 2020 and could not give any time-frame within which he might feel well enough to depart Australia, the Tribunal considers the applicant is seeking to use the subclass 600 Visitor visa to establish de facto residence in Australia. Consequently, the Tribunal is not satisfied that the visa applicant genuinely intends to stay temporarily in Australia for the purpose for which the visa would be granted.

Mohamed and Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (Migration)

10 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3606Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationMigration
Mr Mohamed sought review of a delegate’s refusal of his Partner Visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the refusal notice was emailed to his nominated address on 18 June 2024 and deemed received that day, so his 26 August 2024 review application was about two months outside the mandatory nine-day period in s 500(6B). It held it had no jurisdiction and dismissed the application under s 42A(4) of the Administrative Appeals Tribunal Act 1975 (Cth).
Key holding

A s 501G notice sent by email to the recipient’s designated address is taken to be received at the end of the day of transmission, commencing the nine-day review period under s 500(6B).

He was therefore taken to have received it by the end of that day. The nine-day time limit for an appeal then began to run and Mr Mohamed had until 27 June 2024 to lodge his review application but did not do so until 26 August 2024, approximately two months later.

Huynh (Migration)

9 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3522Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Justine Clarke
Huynh concerns a refusal of an Other Family (Migrant) (Class BO) visa, specifically the Subclass 115 (Remaining Relative) visa, to a Vietnamese applicant sponsored by her brother in Australia. Although the brother was accepted as an Australian relative usually resident in Australia, the applicant’s mother was usually resident in Vietnam and not an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen at the time of application.
Key holding

For a Subclass 115 visa, because cl 115.221 requires the applicant to continue to satisfy cl 115.211, a failure to meet reg 1.15(1)(c) at the time of application cannot be cured by later circumstances.

In effect, the use of the word 'continues' in this clause necessitates that a visa applicant has met the criterion in cl 115.211. Clause 115.211 is a time of application criterion which requires that, at the time a visa applicant applies for the Subclass 115 visa, they are 'a remaining relative of an Australian relative for the applicant'.

THE HOUR GLASS (AUSTRALIA) PTY LTD (Migration)

Before: Andrew McLean Williams
The Hour Glass (Australia) Pty Ltd sought review of a delegate’s refusal to approve a nomination for a Subclass 482 visa in the Short-term stream. Alvindo (Migration)

9 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3378Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationMigration
Before: David McCulloch
Alvindo concerns review of a delegate’s decision to cancel Mr Alvindo’s Subclass 500 (Student) visa after he was convicted of knowingly possessing child abuse material and two optical surveillance device offences. The Tribunal found the conviction ground was made out but affirmed cancellation after weighing the serious privacy offences against his study record, remorse and hardship. It is a discretionary migration cancellation decision.
Key holding

A conviction for an offence against a Commonwealth, State or Territory law is a prescribed ground for cancellation under s 116(1)(g), and where s 116(3) does not mandate cancellation the Tribunal must exercise the cancellation discretion.

For these reasons, the Tribunal is satisfied that the ground for cancellation in s 116(1)(g) exists. As that ground does not require mandatory cancellation under s 116(3), the Tribunal must proceed to consider whether the visa should be cancelled.

9 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3264Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
The applicant, a UK-born minor, applied for Australian citizenship by descent through his mother, an Australian citizen by descent. A delegate refused the application because the mother had not been present in Australia for the required two years (730 days) before the application. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no discretion to overcome the shortfall.
Key holding

Under s 16(2)(b)(i) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), the two-year presence requirement is mandatory and the Minister or Tribunal has no discretion to approve citizenship by descent if it is not met.

There is no discretion available to the Minister with respect to an Applicant not meeting the requirements of section 16(2) of the Act. If these prescriptive legislative requirements are not able to be met, the citizenship application cannot be approved.

Vani and Minister for Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Citizenship)

6 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3180Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Stanley Vani applied for Australian citizenship by descent based on his father’s claimed Aboriginal Australian status, which he said would avoid the effect of s 65(1) of the PNG Constitution. The Tribunal found the Applicant’s father did not satisfy the tripartite test for Aboriginality as at PNG Independence Day, 16 September 1975. Key holding

To establish Aboriginal Australian status, a person must satisfy the tripartite test of biological descent, self-identification, and mutual recognition by elders or others with traditional authority, with mutual recognition requiring authority sourced in pre-European settlement norms.

Membership of the indigenous people depends on biological descent from the indigenous people and on mutual recognition of a particular person's membership by that person and by the elders or other persons enjoying traditional authority among those people.

Key holding

In a s 501CA review, the Tribunal cannot go behind the essential facts of the conviction and sentence that founded the mandatory cancellation, and an applicant bears a heavy onus to challenge those facts.

Moreover, the Applicant has not discharged what would otherwise be his "heavy onus" to challenge the facts upon which the conviction and sentence are necessarily based as set out above.

Miss Make Liku Movono held a Subclass 500 (Student) visa. A delegate cancelled it because she was not enrolled in a full-time registered course from 9 August 2021, breaching condition 8202(2)(a). The Tribunal reviewed the cancellation and affirmed it, finding significant non-enrolment and no extenuating or compassionate circumstances.
Key holding

A breach of student visa condition 8202(2)(a) by failing to be enrolled in a full-time registered course establishes the discretionary cancellation ground under s 116(1)(b), which is not mandatory under s 116(3) and therefore requires consideration of the discretion to cancel.

For these reasons, the Tribunal is satisfied that the ground for cancellation in s 116(1)(b) exists. As that ground does not require mandatory cancellation under s 116(3), the Tribunal must proceed to consider whether to exercise its discretion to cancel the visa.

Khendo Sherpa (Migration)

31 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3393Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Christine Kannis
The Tribunal affirmed cancellation of Ms Dawa Khendo Sherpa’s Subclass 500 (Student) visa (Class TU) because she was not enrolled in a full-time registered course from 11 March 2021 to 8 June 2023. The Tribunal found breach of condition 8202(2)(a) and, after considering discretionary factors, declined to set aside cancellation.
Key holding

Condition 8202(2)(a) imposes a continuing requirement that a student visa holder remain enrolled in a full-time registered course, so even a temporary gap in enrolment breaches the condition.

Condition 8202(2)(a) requires that the holder be enrolled and the enrolment requirement is a continuing requirement and does not allow the visa holder to cease to be enrolled in a course, even to the extent of a temporary gap in enrolment.

Lin (Migration)

31 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3390Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationMigration
Before: Christine Kannis
The Tribunal affirmed cancellation of Mr Lin’s Class TU (Subclass 500) student visa because he was not enrolled in a full-time registered course from 19 November 2021 to 12 March 2023. He claimed a former migration agent failed to pay course fees, but the Tribunal found no probative evidence and held he remained responsible for maintaining enrolment. The cancellation was affirmed on discretion.
Key holding

A student visa holder is personally responsible for understanding and complying with visa conditions, including maintaining enrolment and checking that tuition fees have been paid, and reliance on a migration agent does not excuse non-compliance.

The Tribunal notes that even if the applicant had an agent who assisted him, that does not diminish his own responsibility to check that his fees have been paid. In the Tribunal's view it is the responsibility of a visa holder to be aware of the conditions of their visa and remain compliant with them.

2405987 (Refugee)

30 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4154Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Khanh Hoang
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to a Vanuatu citizen who claimed family land inheritance disputes, political tensions and black magic threats. It accepted some family tension and threats but found he could safely return to Port Vila, where he had lived for about a decade, and affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

A well-founded fear of persecution requires a real chance that is not remote or far-fetched, and the chance may be below 50 per cent.

A 'real chance' is one that is not remote or insubstantial or a far-fetched possibility. A person can have a well-founded fear of persecution even though the possibility of the persecution occurring is well below 50 per cent: Chan Yee Kin v MIEA (1989) 169 CLR 379.

Where an applicant’s review application has been dismissed for non-appearance and no reinstatement application is made within the statutory 14-day period, the Tribunal must confirm the dismissal and the underlying decision is taken to be affirmed.

Where a cancellation ground under s 116(1)(b) is established, the decision-maker must still decide whether the visa should be cancelled by weighing all relevant circumstances, including policy.

Araoz (Migration)

30 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3174Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: David Barker
Mrs Claudia Araoz sought review of a delegate’s refusal of a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) visa. Although the delegate refused for not being a genuine temporary entrant, the Tribunal considered whether she met the current enrolment requirement. Because she did not respond to Tribunal invitations and PRISMS showed no current Confirmation of Enrolment, the Tribunal affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

The Tribunal treats PRISMS as a reliable record of a visa applicant’s enrolment unless there is specific evidence to the contrary.

While it is possible providers may not update PRISMS as required, the Tribunal accepts that PRISMS is a reliable record of enrolments unless there is specific evidence to the contrary in relation to a particular case. There is no such evidence in this case.

2429454 (Migration)

30 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3172Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Anne Grant
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal to grant a Bridging E (Class WE) visa, where the applicant wanted to remain in Australia for criminal hearings and relied on having acceptable arrangements to depart. The Tribunal was not satisfied he met cl 050.212(2) or any other alternative criterion, and affirmed the refusal. It also found he did not meet Subclass 051 criteria.
Key holding

For cl 050.212(2), a bare assertion of third-party financial assistance, without evidence of the supporter’s willingness and capacity, is insufficient to establish acceptable arrangements to depart Australia.

A simple assertion that someone will help with flight purchases and financial support, without any confirmation demonstrating that the supporting person is willing and has the capacity to do so is insufficient, in my view, to be considered 'appropriate arrangements' for departure.

Employment discrimination causing only relative economic disadvantage, without serious harm as defined in s 5J(5), does not establish a well-founded fear of persecution.

Before: Fraser Robertson
This is an AATA review of a delegate’s refusal to grant protection visas to a married Macedonian couple. They claimed to fear harm from a March 2018 armed attack allegedly linked to Applicant 1’s brief service in the 2001 Macedonian conflict, plus Applicant 2’s mental health and work capacity. The Tribunal accepted some background but rejected the claimed attack as implausible and affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

A decision-maker assessing complementary protection may rely on relevant findings made in the refugee assessment where the factual bases overlap.

To the extent that the factual bases for claims under s 36(2)(a) and s 36(2)(aa) overlap, a decision-maker, when considering the complementary protection criterion under s 36(2)(aa), is entitled to refer to and rely on any relevant findings the decision-maker made when considering the refugee criterion under s 36(2)(a).

Before: Peter Katsambanis
The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction to review a refusal of a protection visa because the review application was lodged late. The delegate refused the visa on 6 April 2024, but the applicant did not lodge her review until 10 May 2024, outside the 28-day period.
Key holding

For a protection visa review where the applicant is not in immigration detention, the application must be lodged within 28 days starting on the day of notification; if lodged late, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction.

As the applicant was not in immigration detention on the day the applicant was notified of the decision, an application for review of the decision had to be made within 28 days, commencing on that day: reg 4.31(2) of the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth) (the Regulations).

Barik (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3417Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Sheridan Aster
The Tribunal considered an application to review a refusal to grant a Training (Class GF) Subclass 407 visa. Because the associated nomination had been refused and the applicant was not nominated by an approved sponsor at the time of the review application, the Tribunal found the visa refusal was not a reviewable decision. The application was therefore dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Key holding

A refusal of a Training (Subclass 407) visa is reviewable only if, at the time of the review application, the applicant has an approved sponsor nomination or has a pending review of the nomination refusal.

A decision to refuse a Training visa is reviewable if the applicant made the visa application while in the migration zone and the applicant is nominated by an approved sponsor at the time the application for review of the visa refusal is made or an application for review of a decision not to approve the nomination has been made but at the time the application for review of the visa refusal is made, review of the decision is pending.

Before: Rosa Gagliardi

The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction because the applicant did not pay the full prescribed review fee within the prescribed period. The applicant had paid part of the fee but declined to pay the balance and sought a refund.
Key holding

A migration review application is not valid, and the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction, where the prescribed fee has not been paid within the prescribed period or any applicable reasonable period after a hardship-reduction determination.

The Tribunal considers the applicant has been given a reasonable period to pay the fee since being notified of the authorised officer's decision; however, the fee has not been paid. The application for review is therefore not a valid application and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction in this matter.

Before: Peter Emmerton
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Employer Nomination (Permanent) (Class EN) Subclass 186 visas in the Temporary Residence Transition stream because the primary applicant, a chef, could not demonstrate competent English at the time of application. Jiang (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3198Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Tania Flood
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Ms Jiang’s Visitor (Class FA) Subclass 600 visa because she applied after her substantive visa expired. It found the late application resulted from forgetfulness and inadequate reminders, not factors beyond her control under Schedule 3 criterion 3004(c). The applicant was also offshore at the time of decision, so cl 600.411 was not met.
Key holding

Under criterion 3004(c), whether the applicant ceased to hold a substantive visa because of factors beyond their control is assessed subjectively and practically, and forgetfulness or failure to take available compliance measures will not ordinarily qualify.

The test is in that sense "subjective" rather than being directed at deciding what would have been beyond the control of an abstract or "reasonable" person. A second point is that what is "beyond control" should be tested by considering whether the happening of the event was or was not within the control of the applicant in a practical or realistic sense.

2411742 (Refugee)

27 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4375Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewVisa integrityMigration
Before: Damian Creedon
The applicant is an older South Korean citizen who claimed protection in Australia because he feared being unable to find work in South Korea due to age discrimination and long absence. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal of his protection visa, finding South Korea offers effective protection against age discrimination and that his economic/employment concerns did not meet protection criteria.
Key holding

Effective protection measures available from the receiving State can negate a well-founded fear of persecution under s 5J(2).

The Tribunal finds, therefore, that South Korea can offer effective protection to its citizens against age discrimination. It follows, and the Tribunal finds, that effective protection measures against age discrimination are available to the applicant in South Korea, and that therefore he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on that ground: s 5J(2).
